study.title: 1 Samuel 20 David and Jonathan renew the covenant before Saul's hostility
study.overview: This chapter shows David and Jonathan dealing with Saul's growing decision to kill David. The text highlights David's honesty in exposing his anguish, Jonathan's allegiance by confirming the danger, the use of a combined sign to communicate the truth without exposing David, and the painful separation between the two friends. At the same time, the chapter reveals how the covenant made in the name of the Lord guides the friendship, protection and future hope of David's house. The conflict is not only personal: Saul's opposition to God's anointed is already advancing toward an irreversible break.

outline.title: David exposes his situation and seeks clarity
outline.explanation: David flees from Naioth in Ramah and seeks Jonathan, asking which sin he would have committed for Saul to seek his life. Jonathan, however, still believes that Saul does not intend to kill him and thinks that the king would tell him anything important. David insists that the danger is real and proposes a plan to discover Saul's intention during the feast of the new moon.

outline.title: Jonathan and David covenant stand before the Lord again
outline.explanation: The two go into the field, and Jonathan invokes the LORD as a witness of his promise. He commits himself to informing David of the outcome of the investigation and desires that the Lord be with David as he was with Saul. The covenant is extended to include David's house, with the request for continual mercy for the descent of Jonathan.

outline.title: Saul reveals his hostility against David and smites his son's loyalty
outline.explanation: At the feast of the new moon, David's place is empty. On the first day Saul does not comment, but in the second question why David did not come. Jonathan repeats the combined excuse, Saul infuriates against him, accuses him of choosing David instead of the house's own honor and states that David must die. When Jonathan protests, Saul throws a spear against him; so Jonathan realizes his father's determination.

outline.title: The Sign of Escape and Farewell in Peace
outline.explanation: Jonathan goes to the field on the combined day, fire arrows beyond the boy who accompanies him and gives the secret sign to David understand that he needs to flee. Then he sends the servant back to the city, finds David, and the two say goodbye to crying, reverence and renewal of the compromise. Jonathan closes the meeting by declaring peace and reaffirming the perpetual bond between his descendants under the name of the Lord.

study.context: The chapter mentions a celebration of the new moon, linked to the lunar calendar of the Hebrews and a special sacrifice at the beginning of each month. This detail explains why David's absence would be quickly noticed. The text also shows that certain ritual conditions could make someone ceremonially unclean and unable to participate in a sacred feast at that moment, which makes verossimil the excuse used by Jonathan. The immediate backdrop is the tension between Saul and David, which is already growing in the previous chapters, and now confirmed within the royal family itself.
study.theology: The chapter presents the fidelity of God acting amidst human fragility. First, the covenant between David and Jonathan is made before the LORD, showing that true allegiance is not only sentimental, but moral and spiritual. Second, friendship is tested by truth: Jonathan does not protect his father from the justice of the fact, but also does not abandon the friend to violence. Third, the text anticipates the preservation of the house of David, for Jonathan asks for mercy for his offspring, recognizing that the future belongs to the purpose of God, not to political rivalry. Finally, Saul's refusal to repent reveals how jealousy hardens the heart and destroys relations, even the connection between father and son. The chapter thus counters two covenants: the fraternal covenant under the name of the LORD and the stubborn hostility of Saul against God's chosen one.

scholarViews.insight: The reference to the new moon indicates a monthly feast of the old Hebrew calendar, started with special sacrifice; this explains why David's absence would be perceived in the festive meal.
Jonathan is shown as a faithful friend who solemnly renews his friendship with David, not by mere affection, but to establish allegiance before God in the midst of danger.
The exit to the field and the use of the sign of arrows serve to communicate to David safely the intention of Saul without exposing the plan to the boy who accompanied Jonathan.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the difference between true loyalty and political convenience?
How does the friendship between David and Jonathan show that fidelity to God can demand difficult conversations and painful decisions?
How does Saul's hardening alert the believer to the danger of jealousy and refusal to submit to the will of God?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to cultivate friendships that say the truth, protect others and remain faithful before God. It also teaches us to perceive when a situation is no longer secure and seeks wisdom, without confusing courage with recklessness. In practice, it is worth examining whether we have kept promises, spoken honestly and treated the future of others with mercy. Prayer and covenant with the Lord must guide both the way we face conflicts and the way we farewell when the path separates.
study.uncertainty: The text of the notes does not inform additional details about the exact chronology of these events nor allow to state historically accurately beyond what the chapter itself and the comments provide. The explanation of ceremonial impurity and the feast of the new moon is inferred from the notes mentioned; one should not exaggerate beyond them. It is also not possible to determine, only with this material, all the internal feelings of each character, except where the text itself manifests them.
